questions.q: Why does this lesson say "just connect Salesforce to the ERP" is not a usable requirement on its own?
options: It bundles several data elements with different volatility and ownership into one vague ask, instead of naming a system of record and pattern per field
Salesforce cannot technically connect to any on-premises system under any circumstances
ERPs never expose any kind of integration endpoint
Sales reps are not allowed to see ERP data for compliance reasons
questions.explain: The phrase hides several distinct data elements (catalog, inventory, credit hold, quoting) with different volatility and ownership. An architect has to unbundle it into field-by-field decisions before any technology choice makes sense.

questions.q: At Meridian Fixtures, which system is authoritative for current on-hand inventory, per this case study's analysis?
options: Salesforce, because reps need to be able to override it on a quote
The ERP, because inventory is consumed across multiple channels and changes constantly outside of Salesforce
Neither system — inventory is tracked in a separate spreadsheet
Whichever system the customer's purchase order specifies
questions.explain: The ERP is authoritative for inventory because stock is consumed by multiple channels and changes by the minute — Salesforce has no independent way to know the real number.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a synchronous request-reply callout for inventory and credit hold, but a scheduled batch sync for product catalog and price?
options: Batch sync is always cheaper, so it should be used whenever possible regardless of the data
Inventory and credit hold change too fast and matter too much for staleness, while catalog/price changes rarely enough that a live callout would add latency for no benefit
Salesforce cannot store catalog or price data locally under any design
Named Credentials only work with batch jobs, never with real-time callouts
questions.explain: The deciding factor is data volatility and tolerance for staleness: fast-changing, high-stakes fields (inventory, credit hold) justify a live callout, while slow-changing fields (catalog, price) are better served by a cached batch sync that avoids unnecessary real-time load.

questions.q: In this lesson's design, what is a Named Credential used for?
options: Storing a sales rep's personal login to the ERP
Centrally managing the ERP endpoint URL and authentication so it isn't hardcoded into the integration logic
Encrypting data at rest inside the ERP database
Replacing the need for any system-of-record decision
questions.explain: A Named Credential lets the real-time callout reference a centrally managed endpoint and authentication setup instead of hardcoding a URL or secret directly in the integration code.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a workable design must state about the real-time inventory callout, beyond just making the call?
options: Nothing — real-time callouts never fail in production
A fallback behavior for when the ERP is slow or unreachable, such as showing a last-synced number with a visible timestamp instead of blocking the quote screen entirely
That the feature should simply be removed if the ERP is ever down
That reps should call the warehouse by phone whenever the callout fails
questions.explain: A workable design names a fallback for the callout's failure case up front — showing the last-synced value with an "as of" timestamp — rather than letting an ERP outage block sales reps from working at all.
